evidence: On April 18, 2025, Mohammed H., a 20-year-old Bangladeshi national studying Management Information Systems at Minnesota State University, Mankato, filed a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 challenging his detention by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The petitioner had lawfully entered the United States in 2021 on an F-1 student visa and was in good academic standing.
He had made social media posts expressing support for Palestinian human rights and opposing violence in Gaza.

On March 22, 2025, DHS contacted the State Department seeking revocation of the petitioner's visa, citing a 2023 misdemeanor disorderly conduct charge for which he had already completed a stayed sentence and probation.
The State Department revoked his visa on March 23, citing public safety concerns.
On March 28, 2025, DHS officers arrested the petitioner outside his home and terminated his Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) record.
The initial charging document cited failure to maintain status, though this was later changed to visa revocation nearly a month after his arrest.
An Immigration Judge held a bond hearing on April 9, 2025, and found that the petitioner posed no danger to the community, ordering his release on a $7,500 bond.
However, DHS immediately appealed and invoked an automatic stay under 8 C.F.R. § 1003.19(i)(2), keeping him detained without any individualized showing of danger or flight risk.
The petitioner claimed his detention violated the First Amendment's protection of free speech, the Fifth Amendment's guarantee of due process, and the Administrative Procedure Act.
Judge Jerry W. Blackwell granted a temporary restraining order on April 22, 2025, preventing the government from transferring the petitioner out of Minnesota.

After briefing from both sides, the court ordered the petitioner's release on bail on May 5, 2025, finding he had shown substantial constitutional claims and exceptional circumstances including untreated medical conditions (multiple hernias requiring surgery).
On June 17, 2025, Judge Blackwell granted the habeas petition on all three claims.

The court found the government violated the First Amendment by targeting the petitioner for his protected political speech about Palestine, noting the lack of any explanation for why DHS initiated a criminal records search or contacted the State Department about him in the first place.

The court determined the government's shifting justifications and failure to rebut the temporal connection between the petitioner's speech and his arrest established retaliatory motive by a preponderance of evidence.
The court also found Fifth Amendment violations both in the punitive nature of the detention and in the government's use of the automatic stay provision without any individualized justification.

Finally, the court held that terminating the petitioner's SEVIS record violated the Administrative Procedure Act because none of the cited reasons—visa revocation, criminal record, failure to maintain status, or foreign policy—provided a lawful basis under federal regulations.
The court ordered the petitioner to remain released on the previously imposed conditions including the $7,500 bond.

evidence: On March 17, 2025, Erie County, New York filed suit against the Corporation for National and Community Service (AmeriCorps) and its interim agency head Jennifer Bastress Tahmasebi, challenging new grant certification requirements imposed following executive orders on diversity, equity, and inclusion programs.
The county was represented by private counsel from Gerstein Harrow LLP.
The case was assigned to Chief Judge James E. Boasberg.
Erie County had applied for and received a three-year Retired and Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP) grant from AmeriCorps worth approximately $250,000, with approval granted in January 2024.
The grant supported senior volunteer services in the Buffalo area, including Meals on Wheels programs.

Since 1999, AmeriCorps regulations have required RSVP grantees to establish Advisory Councils 'of a diverse composition that reflects the demographics of the service area,' and Erie County's grant application described efforts to recruit diverse volunteers and advisory board members in compliance with these requirements.

Following Executive Orders 14151 and 14173 signed by President Trump on January 20-21, 2025, which directed federal agencies to eliminate DEI programs and equity-related grants, AmeriCorps sent Erie County a letter on February 14, 2025.

The letter identified terms like 'diversity,' 'equity,' and 'DEI' in the county's grant application and required Erie County to either certify that its program 'does not include any activities that promote DEI activities,' amend its grant to remove such language, or relinquish the award.
The agency warned that non-response could result in termination of the grant.

Erie County brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging that AmeriCorps' actions were arbitrary and capricious because they violated the agency's own regulations requiring diversity, and under the Spending Clause, arguing the new requirements imposed unconstitutionally vague conditions on federal funding.
The county sought injunctive and declaratory relief to prevent AmeriCorps from enforcing the new certification requirements.
On March 21, 2025, Erie County filed a motion for preliminary injunction seeking to compel AmeriCorps to determine the county was in compliance without requiring the DEI certification.

The motion referenced a related case, National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education v. Trump, in which a Maryland federal court had issued a preliminary injunction against enforcement of the executive orders, though that injunction was later stayed by the Fourth Circuit on March 18, 2025.

AmeriCorps filed its opposition on April 4, 2025, arguing that Erie County faced no imminent irreparable harm, that the court lacked jurisdiction over what was essentially a contract dispute, and that the claims were not ripe.

On April 14, 2025, before the scheduled April 25 hearing on the preliminary injunction motion, Erie County voluntarily dismissed the case without prejudice, stating that AmeriCorps had changed its certification requirements since the filing of the suit.

evidence: On March 14, 2025, twelve career civil servants employed by the Department of Veterans Affairs filed this action against Secretary Douglas A. Collins, challenging their designation as "DEIA employees" and the closure of their office.
The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act and the First and Fifth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief.

They argued that their office's mission—identifying and addressing disparities in veterans' access to benefits—was fundamentally different from traditional diversity, equity, and inclusion work, making their designation as "DEIA employees" erroneous and retaliatory.
The case arose from Executive Order 14151, signed by President Trump on January 20, 2025, which ordered the termination of all DEI and DEIA offices in the federal government.

On January 22, 2025, Acting VA Secretary Todd B. Hunter sent an agency-wide email announcing the closure of all DEIA offices, stating these programs "divided Americans by race, wasted taxpayer dollars, and resulted in shameful discrimination."
That same day, all twenty-seven OEA employees were placed on administrative leave and lost access to VA systems.

According to the complaint's factual allegations, OEA's work focused on ensuring equitable delivery of VA benefits to all veterans, particularly addressing challenges faced by rural veterans, those in geographically disadvantaged areas like Puerto Rico and Hawaii, and validating findings from a Government Accountability Office report on disparities in benefit grants.
On February 14, 2025, the plaintiffs received termination notices effective immediately through a Specific Reduction in Force, though these notices were issued after the stated effective time.
On February 27, 2025, their terminations were rescinded and they were retroactively placed back on administrative leave.
On March 13, 2025, they received new Specific Reduction in Force notices scheduling their separation for May 10, 2025.
On April 18, 2025, the plaintiffs filed a motion for a temporary restraining order to enjoin their designation as DEIA employees and restore their access to VA systems and benefits.
The government opposed the motion, arguing that the Civil Service Reform Act precluded judicial review and that the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their constitutional claims in district court.
Following a hearing on May 2, 2025, Judge Contreras denied the TRO for reasons stated on the record.

The plaintiffs alleged that being labeled as DEIA employees who engaged in "wasteful" and "shameful" work constituted viewpoint discrimination and retaliation in violation of the First Amendment, denied them due process under the Fifth Amendment, and violated equal protection principles.
On July 17, 2025, the plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed the case without prejudice, leaving open the possibility of refiling their claims at a later date.
Despite VBA leadership's attempts to reassign the OEA staff to other positions within the agency where vacancies existed, the Office of Personnel Management directed that all employees be terminated.

evidence: On March 5, 2025, BlueRibbon Coalition, Inc. (a nonprofit organization advocating for outdoor recreation access), Sage Riders Motorcycle Club (a Utah-based group with over 200 members), and Paul Wells (a member of both organizations) filed suit against the Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Department of the Interior in the District of Utah, challenging the agencies' December 31, 2024 San Rafael Swell Travel Management Plan.

The plaintiffs, represented by BlueRibbon Coalition attorney Isabella Eldridge, brought their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, alleging violations of the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the APA itself.

The challenged travel plan affects approximately 1.3 million acres in Emery County, Utah, with BLM managing about 1.15 million of those acres. The plan closed 665 miles of previously available routes to motorized recreation while designating 1,496 miles for off‑highway vehicle use, representing a net increase of 67 miles compared to the 2008 plan.

This travel planning process arose from a 2017 settlement agreement in prior litigation (Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance v. U.S. Department of the Interior) in which BlueRibbon had intervened, requiring BLM to develop new travel management plans for multiple areas including the San Rafael Swell.

The plaintiffs assert three main legal theories. First, they claim BLM's route closures violate the Dingell Act by creating impermissible 'buffer zones' around congressionally designated wilderness areas and establishing a de facto wild river designation for the Price River without congressional authorization. They point to specific route closures near Sid's Mountains, Mexican Mountain Wilderness, and Devil's Canyon Wilderness as examples of unlawful wilderness expansion.

Second, they argue the agency's actions were arbitrary and capricious, citing BLM's failure to respond to significant public comments, inconsistent reasoning for closures (such as claiming 'user conflicts' on routes with documented low use and no reported conflicts), reliance on invalid minimization criteria lacking statutory basis, and the unusual decision to have the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary approve the plan rather than the District Manager, thereby denying plaintiffs the opportunity to appeal to the Interior Board of Land Appeals.

Third, they contend BLM violated NEPA by issuing a Finding of No Significant Impact rather than preparing a full Environmental Impact Statement for a major federal action affecting the human environment.
On March 6, 2025, plaintiffs filed a motion for relief under 5 U.S.C. § 705 or alternatively for a preliminary injunction, seeking to postpone the plan's implementation.
The motion emphasizes irreparable harm from BLM's stated intention to 'obliterate' closed routes through mechanical destruction and revegetation, making them permanently undetectable.

Plaintiff Wells specifically alleges the closures deny him access to his family's historic Marsing Ranch, as routes SS1404, SS1404A, and SS1235 providing direct access were closed, with BLM's suggested alternatives being either miles away, requiring descent from a 1,000‑foot cliff, or crossing private property.

On March 10, 2025, the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance moved to intervene as a defendant, citing its longstanding advocacy in the area and role in the prior litigation that led to this travel planning process.

Despite plaintiffs' opposition, Judge Nuffer granted SUWA's motion to intervene on April 21, 2025, finding SUWA had timely sought intervention, possessed protectable environmental interests that could be impaired, and that these interests might not be adequately represented by the federal defendants given potential policy shifts under the new presidential administration.

The plaintiffs seek declaratory judgment that the travel plan violates federal law, an order setting aside the plan, and a permanent injunction preventing its enforcement. They also request attorney's fees under 28 U.S.C. § 2412.
As of the current scheduling order, the administrative record is due October 31, 2025, with briefing extending through June 2026. The motion for preliminary injunction remains pending.

evidence: On April 7, 2025, an Iranian national working as a software engineer under F-1 student status filed suit under the pseudonym John Doe against President Donald J. Trump, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, Acting ICE Director Todd M. Lyons, and San Francisco ICE Field Office Director Moises Becerra. The plaintiff, represented by private counsel Van Der Hout LLP, brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act and sought declaratory and injunctive relief challenging ICE's termination of his Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) record. The complaint alleged violations of the APA as arbitrary and capricious agency action and violations of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

The plaintiff had come to the United States on an F-1 student visa in 2019, obtained a graduate degree in 2023, and was working pursuant to post-graduate Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) Optional Practical Training (OPT) employment authorization. He was scheduled to change status to H-1B nonimmigrant worker status on June 28, 2025. On March 28, 2025, ICE terminated his SEVIS record, citing INA § 237(a)(1)(C)(i) for "failure to maintain status" and noting he had been "identified in criminal records check." The plaintiff had a single minor misdemeanor conviction that did not constitute a crime of violence and carried a potential sentence of less than one year. DHS had known about this conviction for months and had twice approved immigration benefits applications for the plaintiff after learning of it.

Judge Jeffrey S. White presided over the case. On April 16, 2025, the plaintiff filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order to prevent arrest, detention, transfer, or removal pending litigation. The court granted the TRO ex parte on April 17, 2025, enjoining defendants for fourteen days from taking enforcement action against the plaintiff. Multiple related cases involving similar SEVIS terminations were consolidated with this case, revealing a broader pattern affecting hundreds of international students nationwide, with many cases appearing to target students from African, Arab, Middle Eastern, Muslim, and Asian countries.

During a hearing on April 25, 2025, the government announced that ICE was developing a new policy framework for SEVIS terminations and would reactivate the SEVIS records of affected students, including the plaintiff's, until the new policy was implemented. The court extended the TRO for an additional fourteen days and ordered briefing on preliminary injunction motions. The defendants argued that SEVIS termination does not affect F-1 immigration status and that SEVIS is merely a database for monitoring students, while the plaintiff maintained that the termination violated both the APA and due process rights.

On May 22, 2025, the court granted the plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction, finding at least serious questions on the merits of the APA claims and likelihood of irreparable harm. The defendants filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on July 21, 2025, and subsequently moved to stay the preliminary injunction pending appeal. On August 22, 2025, the court granted the motion to stay in part and denied it in part, allowing some aspects of the preliminary injunction to remain in effect during the appeal.

The case arose in the context of numerous visa revocations and SEVIS terminations that had affected campuses across California and the nation. The plaintiff challenged ICE's authority to terminate SEVIS records without proper grounds or due process, arguing that the agency lacked statutory or regulatory authority for such terminations and that the action violated procedural due process by providing no notice or opportunity to respond before terminating a protected property interest.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I identified the key factual elements that establish the lawsuit, the executive order, the BOP's implementing memoranda, the discontinuation of hormone therapy and social accommodations, and the plaintiffs' claims under the APA, Eighth and Fifth Amendments, and the Rehabilitation Act, as these constitute the factual basis.

evidence: On March 7, 2025, three transgender inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria filed a class action lawsuit challenging Executive Order 14168 and its implementation by the Federal Bureau of Prisons.

The plaintiffs—represented by the ACLU Foundation, Transgender Law Center, and other counsel—are incarcerated individuals who had been receiving hormone therapy and social accommodations (such as gender-affirming clothing and commissary items) to treat their gender dysphoria under longstanding BOP medical policies.

Executive Order 14168, issued on January 20, 2025, prohibits federal funds from being used for 'any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate's appearance to that of the opposite sex.'

Following this order, BOP issued two implementing memoranda in February 2025: the first prohibited purchases of items 'that align with transgender ideology' such as chest binders and gender-specific undergarments, while the second reiterated the funding prohibition for medical treatments.
As a result, the plaintiffs either had their hormone therapy discontinued or were told it would be terminated, and lost access to social accommodations.

The plaintiffs brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act, arguing the BOP's actions were arbitrary and capricious, as well as constitutional claims under the Eighth Amendment (cruel and unusual punishment) and Fifth Amendment (equal protection), and claims under the Rehabilitation Act of 1973.

evidence: On June 3, 2025, Judge Royce C. Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction and certified a class consisting of all current and future BOP inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria. The court found that administrative exhaustion under the Prison Litigation Reform Act was not required because administrative remedies were unavailable at the time of filing—BOP had indicated it lacked authority to provide relief under the executive order. The court determined the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their APA claims, finding that BOP's implementing memoranda failed to provide reasoned explanations for the policy change, did not account for reliance interests of inmates who had been receiving treatment for years, and did not explain how denying this medical care advanced the executive order's stated goals.

The court ordered BOP to make social accommodations available to all class members to the same extent they were available before the executive order, and to provide hormone therapy to class members who had been prescribed such medications. While some plaintiffs had their hormone therapy restored during the litigation, the court found this voluntary cessation did not moot their claims since BOP officials indicated the treatments would be discontinued once the litigation concluded.

evidence: On April 14, 2025, thirty-one international students and recent graduates filed suit against Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons, and Detroit Field Office Director Robert Lynch, challenging the sudden termination of their student records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS).
Beginning around March 28, 2025, the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) unilaterally terminated numerous students' SEVIS records, including those of the plaintiffs.
Rather than being notified by any government agency, the students learned of the terminations through emails from their schools, which discovered the changes during routine SEVIS checks.

The termination reasons recorded in SEVIS generally stated: 'OTHERWISE FAILING TO MAINTAIN STATUS: Individual identified in criminal records check and/or has had their VISA revoked. SEVIS record has been terminated.'
Schools advised affected students to stop working immediately and make arrangements to leave the country.

While all plaintiffs had some contact with the criminal justice system, such as speeding tickets or dismissed charges, none had been convicted of a crime of violence requiring more than one year of imprisonment, nor had any violated immigration laws.

The court determined that the government had no statutory or regulatory authority under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(d) to terminate the students' SEVIS records absent specific qualifying circumstances, none of which applied to the plaintiffs.

Following the TRO, ICE issued a new policy on April 26, 2025, delineating reasons SEVP could terminate SEVIS records, including when 'Evidence of a Failure to Comply with the Terms of Nonimmigrant Status Exists' or upon 'U.S. Department of State Visa Revocation.'

Despite restoring the plaintiffs' records pursuant to the TRO, technical limitations in SEVIS meant the termination history remained visible, showing accumulated out-of-status days for affected students.
The court found irreparable harm in the loss of academic progress, employment authorization, and uncertain legal status that could not be compensated by monetary damages.
Two plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their claims in July 2025.
On July 7, 2025, defendants filed an interlocutory appeal to the Sixth Circuit, assigned case number 25-1611.

The plaintiffs, represented by private counsel, included F-1 academic students and M-1 vocational students from universities across Michigan and nine other states, many of whom were pursuing doctoral degrees or participating in Optional Practical Training (OPT) employment programs.

evidence: On April 10, 2025, four international students enrolled at the University of Michigan and Wayne State University filed suit against the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the Acting Director of U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement, and the Field Office Director of Detroit ICE.

The students—citizens of India, Nepal, and China who had been studying in the United States for two to four years—challenged the Department of Homeland Security's termination of their records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) database, which occurred between April 4 and April 8, 2025.

The SEVIS system showed termination reasons stating 'Individual identified in criminal records check and/or has had their VISA revoked,' though the students maintained they had committed no crimes beyond minor traffic violations.
According to a government declaration, the terminations were based on the students' prior arrests for assault charges (though not all resulted in prosecution) or immigration encounters.

The students alleged that by terminating their SEVIS records, the government had also terminated their F-1 student status, thereby violating the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause and the Administrative Procedure Act. They claimed the terminations occurred without notice, explanation, or opportunity to respond.
Following a hearing on April 15, 2025, Judge Stephen J. Murphy III denied the motion for a temporary restraining order on April 17, 2025.
The government argued that terminating a SEVIS record—which it characterized as merely an administrative database entry—does not automatically terminate F-1 student status.
The parties reached a settlement and filed a stipulated order of dismissal on May 29, 2025.
The students were represented by the American Civil Liberties Union Fund of Michigan and cooperating attorneys from private practice.

The government argued that terminating a SEVIS record—which it characterized as merely an administrative database entry—does not automatically terminate F‑1 status. evidence: On April 9, 2025, two Northwestern University law professors filed suit against the U.S. House Committee on Education and Workforce and its leadership, challenging document demands that allegedly violated their constitutional rights.

The professors—Sheila Bedi, who directs the Community Justice and Civil Rights Clinic, and Lynn Cohn, who teaches at the Center on Negotiation, Mediation, and Restorative Justice—work at Northwestern's Bluhm Legal Clinic, which provides pro bono legal services through various clinical programs.
The lawsuit arose from a March 27, 2025 letter from the Committee demanding that Northwestern produce extensive documents by April 10, 2025 at 11:00 AM Central Time.

The Committee specifically targeted Professor Bedi's representation of protesters who participated in a 2024 pro-Palestinian demonstration that blocked access to O'Hare Airport, characterizing her work as "troubling" and describing Northwestern Law School as engaging in "left-wing political activism."

The demanded documents included detailed budgets for all twenty clinics and twelve centers within the Bluhm Legal Clinic, complete donor lists, records of payments to outside parties since 2020, and all of Professor Bedi's hiring materials and performance reviews.
The professors alleged that the Committee's demands violated their First Amendment rights to free speech, freedom of association, academic freedom, and petition for redress of grievances.

They claimed the Committee was engaging in viewpoint discrimination by explicitly targeting what it called "left-wing advocacy" and "progressive-left political advocacy," using a purported investigation into antisemitism as pretext.
The complaint also raised Fifth Amendment due process and equal protection claims, as well as Sixth Amendment concerns about interference with attorney-client relationships.

The professors argued that compliance would cause irreparable harm by chilling their speech, deterring donors and clients, compromising attorney-client confidentiality, and exposing sensitive information about their legal strategies and funding.

On April 10, 2025, Judge Andrea Wood held an emergency hearing via videoconference. During the hearing, the Committee's counsel withdrew the document demands, rendering the temporary restraining order request moot.
The court denied the motion without prejudice as moot.

Subsequently, on June 20, 2025, the parties filed a joint motion to stay the proceedings, which Judge Elaine Bucklo granted on June 24, 2025, staying the case until further order of the court with a status report due September 15, 2025.

The lawsuit stemmed from a March 27, 2025 letter demanding that Northwestern produce extensive documents by April 10, 2025. The Committee specifically targeted Professor Bedi’s representation of protesters who participated in a 2024 pro‑Palestinian demonstration that blocked access to O'Hare Airport, calling her work troubling and describing Northwestern Law School as left‑wing political activism. The demanded documents included budgets for all twenty clinics and twelve centers within the Bluhm Legal Clinic, donor lists, records of payments to outside parties since 2020, and Professor Bedi’s hiring materials and performance reviews. The professors alleged that the demands violated their First Amendment rights (free speech, freedom of association, academic freedom, petition for redress) and constituted viewpoint discrimination, and they raised Fifth Amendment due process, equal protection, and Sixth Amendment attorney‑client confidentiality claims. The lawsuit was filed as part of an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order represented by the Center for Constitutional Rights and private counsel, and Northwestern University, its president, and board chair were named as nominal defendants because they received the Committee’s demands. On April 10, 2025, Judge Andrea Wood held an emergency hearing via videoconference; the Committee withdrew the demands, rendering the temporary restraining order moot. The court denied the motion without prejudice as moot. On June 20, 2025, the parties filed a joint motion to stay the proceedings, which Judge Elaine Bucklo granted on June 24, 2025, staying the case until further order with a status report due September 15, 2025.

evidence: On April 23, 2025, the American Bar Association filed suit against the U.S. Department of Justice, Attorney General Pamela J. Bondi, and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche in their official capacities, represented by the Democracy Forward Foundation.

The case arose from DOJ's termination of five Office on Violence Against Women grants totaling $3.2 million that funded the ABA's Commission on Domestic and Sexual Violence, which provides training and technical assistance to legal professionals working with survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking.

The dispute began after the ABA publicly criticized the Trump Administration's actions regarding the judiciary and legal profession in February and March 2025, and joined a lawsuit challenging the Administration's freeze on international development grants.

On April 9, 2025, Deputy Attorney General Blanche issued a memorandum to all DOJ employees citing the ABA's litigation against the government and announcing new restrictions: prohibiting DOJ employees from participating in ABA events on official time, barring use of taxpayer funds for ABA-related travel, and requiring policy employees to obtain approval before any ABA engagement.
The next day, DOJ terminated all of the ABA's OVW grants "effective immediately," citing changed "agency priorities" without further explanation.
DOJ terminated no other OVW grants and assured other grantees their funding was secure.

The ABA's complaint alleges violations of the First Amendment (retaliation for protected speech, viewpoint discrimination, and unconstitutional conditions on government grants), Fifth Amendment Equal Protection and Due Process violations, and violations of the Administrative Procedure Act.

The ABA sought declaratory and injunctive relief, including a temporary restraining order or preliminary injunction to prevent enforcement of the grant terminations and require continued disbursement of funds.
The government moved to dismiss, arguing primarily that the Court of Federal Claims had exclusive jurisdiction under the Tucker Act because the case involved cooperative agreements.

Judge Christopher R. Cooper held a hearing on May 12, 2025, and issued a memorandum opinion on May 14, 2025, granting the ABA's motion for preliminary injunction on its First Amendment retaliation claim.

The court found it had jurisdiction because the claim arose from constitutional rights rather than contract terms, and that the ABA was likely to succeed on the merits since DOJ offered no performance-based justification for the terminations and the timing strongly suggested retaliation for protected First Amendment activity.

The court found the ABA would suffer irreparable harm from loss of funding and inability to serve domestic violence survivors, and that the balance of equities and public interest favored maintaining the grants pending resolution of the case.
The court reserved judgment on the ABA's other claims and the remainder of the government's motion to dismiss.

Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: We identified the key factual events: the freeze of foreign aid programs by the Trump administration (via EO 14169 and Secretary Rubio's memo), the lawsuit filed by nonprofits, the alleged statutory violations, the court orders (TRO, preliminary injunction), and the appellate rulings. evidence: On February 10, 2025, two nonprofit organizations that receive federal foreign assistance funding filed suit challenging the Trump administration's freeze of foreign aid programs.

The case arose from Executive Order 14169, issued on President Trump's first day in office on January 20, 2025, which directed an immediate 90-day pause in U.S. foreign development assistance for review of 'programmatic efficiencies and consistency with United States foreign policy.' Four days later, Secretary Rubio issued a memorandum requiring immediate stop-work orders for all existing foreign assistance awards.
These actions immediately halted funding to organizations across the world, causing layoffs, program shutdowns, and disruption of humanitarian services.
AVAC, which had operated for over a decade with PEPFAR funding to support HIV prevention research in African countries, saw its cooperative agreement frozen despite being funded through June 2026.

The organizations alleged these actions violated the Administrative Procedure Act as arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, violated the constitutional separation of powers by usurping Congress's spending power, violated the Take Care Clause, and violated the Impoundment Control Act and Anti-Deficiency Act.

Judge Amir H. Ali granted a temporary restraining order on February 13, 2025, enjoining the defendants (except the President) from enforcing the funding freeze for any foreign assistance awards in existence as of January 19, 2025.

Following a hearing on March 6, the court issued a preliminary injunction on March 10, 2025, finding plaintiffs likely to succeed on their claim that the impoundment of funds violated the separation of powers.

The court ordered defendants to 'make available for obligation the full amount of funds that Congress appropriated for foreign assistance programs' and established a benchmark of processing approximately 300 payments per day for amounts owed.
The government appealed the preliminary injunction on April 1, 2025.

On August 13, 2025, the D.C. Circuit vacated the portion of the preliminary injunction regarding impoundment, holding that plaintiffs lacked a cause of action to enforce the Impoundment Control Act, though Judge Pan dissented.

evidence: On February 4, 2025, PFLAG Inc. (a national LGBTQ+ advocacy organization with over 550,000 members), GLMA (representing healthcare professionals advancing LGBTQ+ equality), six transgender individuals under age nineteen, and four parents filed suit challenging two Executive Orders issued by President Trump.
The plaintiffs are represented by the American Civil Liberties Union and Lambda Legal Defense and Education Fund.
The case was assigned to Judge Brendan Abell Hurson in the District of Maryland.
Executive Order 14,168 ('Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism'), issued January 20, 2025, which declares that federal funds shall not be used to promote 'gender ideology'.

Executive Order 14,187 ('Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation'), issued January 28, 2025, which directs federal agencies to immediately ensure that institutions receiving federal research or education grants end gender-affirming medical care for people under nineteen.

Within days of their issuance, the Health Resources and Services Administration and Centers for Disease Control sent notices to grant recipients stating that funds supporting programs inconsistent with the Orders were 'terminated in whole or in part'.

Major medical institutions across the country—including Children's National in Washington D.C., Boston Children's Hospital, NYU Langone Health, Denver Health, and numerous others—immediately ceased providing gender-affirming care to patients under nineteen, explicitly citing the Executive Orders and fear of losing federal funding.
The White House issued a press release celebrating these shutdowns as the Orders' 'intended effect'.

The six transgender plaintiff youth, ranging from twelve to eighteen years old, all have gender dysphoria diagnoses and were at various stages of receiving medically necessary treatment when their care was abruptly terminated.
Their treatments included puberty-delaying medications to prevent irreversible physical changes, hormone therapy, and in one case, scheduled surgery.

The sudden cessation of treatment caused documented physical and psychological harm, including increased anxiety, depression, risk of suicide, and the prospect of undergoing irreversible physical changes inconsistent with their gender identity.
After briefing and a lengthy hearing on February 13, 2025, Judge Hurson granted a temporary restraining order, finding plaintiffs demonstrated a strong likelihood of success on all three claims.

The court held that the Executive Orders unconstitutionally usurp Congress's spending power by placing conditions on federal grants that Congress did not authorize, noting that 'there is no provision in the Constitution that authorizes the President to enact, to amend, or to repeal statutes.'

The court also found the Orders likely violate equal protection under controlling Fourth Circuit precedent recognizing that restrictions on gender-affirming care constitute sex-based discrimination requiring heightened scrutiny.
On March 4, 2025, after additional briefing including amicus briefs from multiple states on both sides, the court converted the TRO to a preliminary injunction.

The nationwide injunction prohibits all defendant agencies from conditioning, withholding, or terminating federal funding based on a healthcare entity providing gender-affirming medical care to patients under nineteen.
The injunction specifically covers HHS and all its subagencies, NIH, HRSA, and NSF.

Shortly after the preliminary injunction issued, several HHS subagencies issued new notices threatening future policy changes regarding gender-affirming care, prompting plaintiffs to file an emergency motion to enforce the injunction on March 7, 2025.
The court denied this motion without prejudice on March 28, 2025, finding the agencies had not clearly violated the injunction's specific terms.

Defendants appealed the preliminary injunction to the Fourth Circuit on March 21, 2025, and the parties agreed to stay certain case deadlines pending appeal while preserving plaintiffs' ability to seek enforcement of the injunction or additional relief if needed.

Within days, HHS and CDC sent notices terminating inconsistent federal funds and major hospitals nationwide halted gender-affirming care, prompting the White House to celebrate the shutdowns. The six transgender youth, aged 12 to 18, were receiving puberty blockers, hormones, and planned surgery; abrupt cessation caused increased anxiety, depression, suicide risk, and potential irreversible physical changes. evidence: On April 21, 2020, eight detained individuals at the Prince George's County Jail filed a class action lawsuit against Mary Lou McDonough, the Director of the Prince George's County Department of Corrections, challenging the jail's response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
The plaintiffs—predominantly pretrial detainees plus at least one post-conviction prisoner—were represented by Civil Rights Corps and WilmerHale.

They brought claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 alleging violations of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments' protections against cruel and unusual punishment and denial of due process, as well as a petition for writs of habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 for medically vulnerable detainees.
The plaintiffs alleged that when COVID-19 arrived at the jail (with the first case reported on March 30, 2020), the facility's response violated constitutional standards.

According to the complaint, the jail charged money for soap and limited purchases to one bar per week, required a $4 fee for sick call requests, regularly turned away symptomatic inmates from medical care, and housed COVID-positive prisoners in isolation cells with walls covered in feces, mucus, and blood.
The jail implemented 23‑hour lockdowns confining prisoners to their cells with limited recreation time.

Testing was severely limited—by April 24, only 20 tests had been administered with 18 positive results (a 90% positivity rate)—while 28 staff members had tested positive across thirteen housing units.

The plaintiffs included individuals with serious medical conditions like asthma, chronic bronchitis, and seizure disorders who reported experiencing COVID symptoms but being denied testing or treatment.

Judge Paula Xinis presided over the case and on May 21, 2020, granted a temporary restraining order in part, finding that the jail demonstrated deliberate indifference through three specific failures: undertesting for COVID‑19, inadequate treatment and isolation of symptomatic detainees, and lack of any plan to protect high‑risk detainees.
The order required the jail to submit within five days a comprehensive written plan for identifying, monitoring, treating, and housing detainees at high risk for severe COVID‑19 complications.

The Court appointed Dr. Carlos Franco‑Paredes as an independent inspector, who subsequently found that the jail lacked a functioning protocol for inmates to report grievances and confirmed various deficiencies in the facility's pandemic response.

On July 3, 2020, plaintiffs filed an amended complaint adding two new claims challenging the jail's indefinite lockdown measures as creating unreasonable risks of physical and psychological harm under the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments, and as violating due process by being imposed without adequate procedural protections.

The defendant answered the original complaint but then moved to dismiss the amended complaint in its entirety, arguing mootness for released plaintiffs, failure to exhaust administrative remedies under the Prison Litigation Reform Act, and failure to state claims for relief.
The court's temporary restraining order was allowed to expire, and the parties proceeded to discovery while the motion to dismiss remained pending.
The defendant filed a notice of appeal to the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals, though the scope and status of that appeal is not clear from the available documents.

evidence: On June 20, 2025, five individuals and four organizational plaintiffs filed this action challenging immigration enforcement practices in the Central District of California. The individual plaintiffs are day laborers and workers who were detained by federal agents, while the organizational plaintiffs include the United Farm Workers, the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, and the Immigrant Defenders Law Center.

The case arose from 'Operation At Large,' a large-scale immigration enforcement operation that began in Los Angeles on June 6, 2025. According to the court's findings, federal agents dispatched 'contact teams' of three to five officers to public places such as streets, sidewalks, bus stops, carwashes, and day laborer sites.

The plaintiffs alleged these teams conducted detentive stops without reasonable suspicion in violation of the Fourth Amendment's prohibition against unreasonable seizures. The court found that agents were stopping individuals based solely on factors such as apparent race or ethnicity, speaking Spanish or English with an accent, presence at particular locations, and the type of work they appeared to do. Several plaintiffs described being detained by masked, armed agents who failed to identify themselves as law enforcement.

On July 11, 2025, after full briefing and a hearing, the court granted the plaintiffs' applications for a temporary restraining order. The TRO enjoined defendants from conducting detentive stops in the Central District unless officers had reasonable suspicion that the person to be stopped was in the United States in violation of immigration law. The order specifically prohibited relying solely on the four enumerated factors (race/ethnicity, language, location, or type of work) to form reasonable suspicion, 'except as permitted by law.'

On July 13, 2025, the defendants filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals (Case No. 25-4312) and sought an emergency stay of the TRO. After initially denying the stay motion for procedural deficiencies, the Ninth Circuit held oral argument on July 28, 2025. On August 1, 2025, the appellate court issued a published order partially granting the stay only as to the 'except as permitted by law' clause, which it found impermissibly vague, but otherwise denying the stay and allowing the TRO to remain in effect.

Meanwhile, on July 30, 2025, Magistrate Judge Sheri Pym granted petitioner Carlos Osorto's ex parte application for release from immigration custody. The court found extraordinary circumstances warranted release, noting that the government's inconsistent positions about whether Osorto was entitled to a bond hearing had prevented his release despite the government's concession that he should receive such a hearing. The court ordered Osorto released on a $5,000 bond with ankle monitoring.

The case includes intervention by multiple local governments, including the City of Los Angeles, Los Angeles County, and several other cities, which filed their complaint in intervention on July 29, 2025. A hearing on the plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction and motion for class certification was scheduled for September 24, 2025.

The plaintiffs brought claims under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 (habeas corpus) and alleged violations of the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable seizures and the Fifth Amendment's due process and right to counsel guarantees.

They sought declaratory judgment, injunctive relief, and release from custody for detained individuals. On July 2, 2025, the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint adding class action claims concerning detention conditions and denial of counsel.
extracted.value: The case involves a lawsuit filed on June 20, 2025 by five day laborers and four organizations challenging federal immigration enforcement under Operation At Large, which began on June 6, 2025 and involved federal agents conducting detentions without reasonable suspicion based on race, ethnicity, language, location or type of work; the plaintiffs allege violations of the Fourth and Fifth Amendments and bring habeas corpus claims, seeking declaratory judgment, injunctive relief, and release from custody; a temporary restraining order was granted on July 11, 2025 prohibiting detentions without reasonable suspicion (except as permitted by law); the Ninth Circuit partially granted a stay on August 1, 2025 but the TRO remains effective; additionally, a detainee, Carlos Osorto, was released on bond on July 30, 2025; local governments intervened on July 29, 2025 with a hearing scheduled for September 24, 2025; the plaintiffs also filed an amended complaint on July 2, 2025 adding class action claims concerning detention conditions and denial of counsel.

evidence: On March 12, 2025, two Harvard Medical School professors filed suit challenging the removal of their medical articles from a government-run patient safety website.

The plaintiffs, Dr. Gordon Schiff and Dr. Celeste Royce, sued the U.S. Office of Personnel Management and its Acting Director Charles Ezell, the Department of Health and Human Services and Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and its Acting Director Mamatha S. Pancholi.

The case arose from Executive Order 14168, titled 'Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government,' which President Trump issued on January 20, 2025.
The order directed federal agencies to remove content that 'promote[s] or otherwise inculcate[s] gender ideology.'
OPM issued implementing guidance on January 29, 2025, directing agencies to remove such content from their websites by January 31, 2025.
In response to this directive, AHRQ removed approximately twenty articles from its Patient Safety Network (PSNet) website, including commentaries authored by the plaintiffs.
Dr. Schiff's article on suicide risk assessment had noted that LGBTQ individuals are among high-risk groups for suicide.
Dr. Royce's article on endometriosis diagnosis mentioned that the condition can occur in transgender and non-gender-conforming people.

AHRQ offered to restore the articles only if the authors removed these references, which both doctors refused to do as they considered the information medically accurate and essential for patient safety.

The plaintiffs alleged violations of the First Amendment, claiming the removals constituted viewpoint-based discrimination in a limited public forum, and violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, arguing the agency actions were arbitrary and capricious and that OPM exceeded its statutory authority.
They sought declaratory judgment and injunctive relief to restore their articles and prevent further censorship.

evidence: On April 11, 2025, four Chinese international students filed suit against the Secretary of Homeland Security and Acting Director of ICE challenging the mass termination of their Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) records.

The terminations resulted from ICE running approximately 1.3 million F-1 and M-1 visa holders through the National Crime Information Center database and terminating the SEVIS records of those with any law enforcement contact, regardless of the outcome.
The plaintiffs had no criminal convictions—some had arrests that resulted in dismissed charges or were taken into protective custody, while others had no criminal record whatsoever.
Despite this, their SEVIS records were terminated without prior notice, explanation, or opportunity to contest the decision.

The plaintiffs, represented by the private firm Deheng Law Offices PC and the Chinese American Legal Defense Alliance, brought claims under the Administrative Procedure Act for arbitrary and capricious agency action, and under the Fifth Amendment for violations of due process and equal protection.
Judge Susan Illston initially granted an ex parte temporary restraining order on April 18, 2025, enjoining enforcement of the terminations for the named plaintiffs.
After the TRO was issued, the government announced it was retroactively reactivating all terminated SEVIS records and issued a new policy on April 26, 2025.
The government confirmed that the effect of the retroactive reactivation was 'as though the termination did not happen' with no gaps in the records.
Despite the government's voluntary remedial actions, Judge White granted the plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction on May 22, 2025, issuing nationwide relief.

The injunction prohibited DHS from arresting, incarcerating, or transferring the named plaintiffs and 'similarly situated individuals nationwide,' from imposing any adverse legal effects from the SEVIS terminations, and from reversing the reinstatement of SEVIS records except for reasons specifically authorized by regulation.

The court found the mass terminations likely violated both the APA and due process requirements, noting they were conducted without individualized review or rational connection between the facts and the termination decisions.

The government filed a notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on July 21, 2025, and moved for a stay pending appeal on August 8, 2025, arguing that the nationwide scope of the injunction violated the Supreme Court's June 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA prohibiting universal injunctions.
At the time of the last filed document, approximately 36 additional students from 30 universities had provided declarations supporting the nationwide relief, though no class had been certified.
The case remains pending with the appeal proceeding in the Ninth Circuit.

evidence: On March 24, 2025, three immigrant rights organizations—the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, UndocuBlack Network, and CASA, Inc.—filed suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia challenging Department of Homeland Security policies that expanded expedited removal to include individuals who had been lawfully paroled into the United States at ports of entry.

The lawsuit challenges three specific agency actions taken in early 2025: a January 23 memorandum from Acting DHS Secretary Huffman directing officials to consider applying expedited removal to parolees; a February 18 ICE directive stating there was "no time limit" on processing paroled arriving aliens for expedited removal; and a March 25 Federal Register Notice terminating humanitarian parole programs for nationals of Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela (CHNV).

The plaintiffs alleged these actions violated the Immigration and Nationality Act, specifically 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(1)(A), were arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act, and violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
They brought the case under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(e)(3), which provides jurisdiction in the D.C. District Court for challenges to written policies implementing the expedited removal statute.

The organizations' members include tens of thousands of individuals who were paroled into the United States through various humanitarian programs, including the CHNV parole programs and the CBP One mobile application process. These individuals had fled persecution, violence, and oppressive conditions in their home countries and were granted temporary parole after inspection at U.S. ports of entry. Many had been living in the United States for months or years, obtained work authorization, established families, and were pursuing asylum or other forms of immigration relief through regular removal proceedings.

The case is related to other litigation challenging the expansion of expedited removal (Make the Road New York v. Huffman, No. 25-cv-0190) and the termination of humanitarian parole programs (Svitlana Doe v. Noem, No. 1:25-cv-10495 in the District of Massachusetts).

In the Doe case, a district court had stayed the termination of CHNV parole programs, but the Supreme Court granted an emergency stay of that order on May 30, 2025, allowing the terminations to proceed.

The plaintiffs moved for a stay of the challenged agency actions under 5 U.S.C. § 705 on June 11, 2025. They presented evidence that their members were being arrested at immigration court hearings and CBP checkpoints, detained, and placed in expedited removal proceedings despite having previously been in regular section 240 removal proceedings.

On August 1, 2025, Judge Jia M. Cobb granted the plaintiffs' motion for a stay, finding they were substantially likely to succeed on the merits of their claims that the challenged actions exceeded DHS's statutory authority and were arbitrary and capricious. The court held that neither the "arriving aliens" provision nor the "designation provision" of the expedited removal statute authorized applying expedited removal to individuals who had been paroled into the United States at ports of entry.
The stay applies to all individuals who have been, at any time, paroled into the United States at a port of entry, not just the plaintiffs' members.

The government immediately appealed the stay order to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals on August 5, 2025, and moved for a stay pending appeal, which Judge Cobb denied on August 13, 2025. The appeal remains pending in the D.C. Circuit as Case No. 25-5289.

The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board is an independent agency created by Congress in 2004 following the 9/11 Commission Report to ensure that the government's counterterrorism activities appropriately balance national security needs with privacy and civil liberties protections.

Congress substantially restructured the Board in 2007 after concerns arose about White House interference, including over 200 edits to the Board's first annual report. The 2007 amendments removed the Board from the Executive Office, established it as an independent agency, deleted language stating members served "at the pleasure of the President," added six-year fixed terms, required partisan balance, and mandated that members be selected based on expertise rather than political affiliation.

President Trump also terminated the Board's third Democratic member and Chair, Sharon Bradford Franklin, leaving only Republican member Beth Williams on the five-member Board, thus depriving it of the three-member quorum required to perform its statutory functions.

The case has significant implications for the Board's ability to function, as it cannot meet its statutory obligations without a quorum, including issuing reports to Congress on surveillance programs like Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which is scheduled for reauthorization in 2026.

evidence: On February 13, 2025, twenty-six current and former employees and contractors of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) filed suit against Elon Musk, the United States DOGE Service, and the Department of Government Efficiency, alleging violations of the Appointments Clause and separation of powers principles.

The plaintiffs, represented by the State Democracy Defenders Fund and other public interest counsel, later amended their complaint to add additional defendants including President Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and USAID itself, while reducing the named plaintiffs to six individuals seeking class certification on behalf of all USAID employees.

The case arose from the rapid dismantling of USAID beginning on January 27, 2025, when members of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), created by Executive Order on January 20, 2025, arrived at USAID headquarters and demanded access to all agency systems.

DOGE members, many of whom had previously worked for Musk's companies, gained root-level access to USAID's computer systems, placed 57 senior officials on administrative leave, and began systematically shutting down the agency.
By February 3, 2025, Musk posted on social media that they had "spent the weekend feeding USAID into the wood chipper."

The dismantling included closing USAID's headquarters, removing its website, terminating 2,191 contracts worth $26.1 billion and 2,366 grants worth $41.8 billion, and placing approximately 90% of USAID's 4,765 direct-hire employees on administrative leave.

Plaintiffs alleged that Musk, despite having no formal appointment requiring Senate confirmation, was exercising significant governmental authority as the de facto administrator of DOGE, making decisions to permanently close USAID headquarters and shut down its operations.

They also claimed that the Executive Branch's unilateral dismantling of USAID, a congressionally-created agency, violated separation of powers principles since Congress had not authorized the agency's elimination.
On March 18, 2025, Judge Theodore D. Chuang of the District of Maryland granted a preliminary injunction, finding that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on both constitutional claims.

The injunction prohibited defendants from taking further actions to shut down USAID, required reinstatement of employee access to systems, and mandated that any USAID actions be authorized by a proper USAID official.
The government immediately appealed, and on March 28, 2025, the Fourth Circuit stayed the preliminary injunction pending appeal.

Following the stay, defendants immediately resumed the dismantling process, with most USAID employees receiving termination notices effective July 1, 2025, and Secretary Rubio notifying Congress that substantially all USAID personnel would be separated from federal service.

The case remains pending with a government motion to dismiss arguing that the court lacks jurisdiction due to mandatory statutory review frameworks for federal employment disputes, and plaintiffs' motion for class certification seeking to represent all USAID employees affected by the reorganization.

evidence: On January 28, 2025, eight transgender service members and individuals seeking to enlist filed this constitutional challenge in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia against President Trump's Executive Order 14183 and related policies banning transgender people from military service.

The plaintiffs, represented by GLBTQ Legal Advocates & Defenders and the National Center for Lesbian Rights, include active-duty service members with over 130 years of collective military service and multiple commendations including a Bronze Star.
The defendants are the United States, the Secretary of Defense, and other defense officials in their official capacities.

The plaintiffs alleged violations of the Fifth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, arguing that the executive orders unconstitutionally discriminate against transgender individuals by declaring them inherently incompatible with military service.

Executive Order 14183, issued on January 27, 2025, stated that transgender status is inconsistent with "high standards for troop readiness, lethality, cohesion, honesty, humility, uniformity, and integrity."

The Department of Defense implemented this order through the Hegseth Policy on February 26, 2025, which disqualified transgender individuals from service with only nominal exemptions that virtually no transgender person could meet.
The case was assigned to Judge Ana C. Reyes, who held hearings on the plaintiffs' application for preliminary injunction in February 2025.

The court found that the administration had rushed the policy change—taking only seven days for the executive order and thirty days for implementing guidance, compared to months of study for prior policies.

The court noted that the government provided no evidence of consultation with uniformed military leaders and that supporting documents cited by the administration actually contradicted or failed to support the ban.
On March 18, 2025, Judge Reyes granted the plaintiffs' preliminary injunction, finding they were likely to succeed on their equal protection claim.
The court's 2025 WL 842332 opinion emphasized that the government conceded the plaintiffs were honorable, truthful, disciplined, physically and mentally fit to serve, and had "made America safer."
The injunction maintains the status quo that existed before Executive Order 14183, effectively continuing the Austin Policy that had allowed transgender individuals to serve openly since 2021.
The government moved to dissolve the preliminary injunction on March 21, 2025, citing new guidance that purportedly clarified the policy's scope.
Judge Reyes denied this motion on March 26, 2025 (2025 WL 914716), finding the new guidance did not materially change the discriminatory nature of the ban.

The government then filed an emergency motion for stay pending appeal with the D.C. Circuit on March 27, 2025, arguing that the 2025 policy mirrors the Mattis policy from 2018 that the Supreme Court and D.C. Circuit had previously allowed to take effect in Trump v. Karnoski, 586 U.S. 1124 (2019) and Doe 2 v. Shanahan, 755 F. App'x 19 (D.C. Cir. 2019).

The factual context reveals a history of evolving military policies regarding transgender service. The Carter Policy in 2016 first allowed open service after a comprehensive RAND study found minimal impact on readiness.
The first Trump administration banned such service in 2017, leading to multiple injunctions before the Mattis Policy took effect in 2018.
The Biden administration reversed the ban in 2021 through Executive Order 14004, finding substantial evidence that transgender service did not negatively impact the Armed Forces.

The current challenge addresses the second Trump administration's attempt to reinstate a ban, with the district court finding the new policy was based on conjecture rather than evidence and motivated by unconstitutional animus toward transgender individuals.

evidence: The lawsuit arose from a series of executive orders President Trump issued beginning in February 2025, invoking IEEPA to impose tariffs ranging from 10% to 145% on goods from China and other countries. The President justified these tariffs by declaring national emergencies related to the flow of synthetic opioids from China and 'large and persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficits.' The challenged orders included a February 1 order imposing 10% tariffs on Chinese goods (later raised to 20% on March 3), and an April 2 'Universal and Reciprocal Tariff Order' imposing a baseline 10% tariff on nearly all imports plus additional country-specific tariffs. Factual Basis of Case.reasoning: I identified the key facts, evidence, and background from the summary, extracting the events, evidence items, and contextual information to form a comprehensive factual basis.

evidence: On April 12, 2025, two Venezuelan nationals detained at the ICE Denver Contract Detention Facility filed a class action habeas petition challenging President Trump's use of the Alien Enemies Act to authorize their potential removal from the United States.

The case arose from the President's March 14, 2025 proclamation invoking the Alien Enemies Act of 1798—a wartime authority used only three times in American history—to target members of Tren de Aragua (TdA), a Venezuelan criminal gang.
The proclamation declared that TdA was perpetrating an "invasion" of the United States and authorized the immediate apprehension and removal of Venezuelan nationals alleged to be TdA members.
Related challenges to the proclamation were filed in multiple federal districts, including J.G.G. v. Trump in the District of Columbia and A.A.R.P. v. Trump in the Northern District of Texas.
The Supreme Court had already ruled in J.G.G. that individuals subject to the AEA are entitled to judicial review and adequate notice to seek habeas relief.
Both petitioners were Venezuelan citizens who had entered the United States seeking asylum and were in immigration removal proceedings.
D.B.U. was arrested at what ICE characterized as a "Tren de Aragua party" and interrogated about gang membership, which he denied.
R.M.M. was arrested during an ICE operation and later designated in ICE documents as a "known member" of TdA, though he had actually fled Venezuela after TdA murdered two of his family members.
Neither petitioner had been criminally charged, and both denied any TdA affiliation, though they faced accusations of gang connections in their immigration proceedings.
Judge Charlotte N. Sweeney initially issued an order on April 14, 2025, under the All Writs Act preventing the petitioners' removal pending further proceedings.

After briefing and oral argument, the court granted a temporary restraining order on April 22, 2025 (reported at 2025 WL 1163530), which provisionally certified the class and ordered that the government provide 21-day notice in a language the detainee understands before any removal under the AEA.
The court found that the notice procedures being used—which provided as little as 12 hours' notice in English only—violated due process requirements.
On May 6, 2025, the court certified a class consisting of all noncitizens in custody in the District of Colorado who were, are, or will be subject to the AEA proclamation.
The same day, the court granted a preliminary injunction prohibiting the government from detaining, transferring, or removing class members from the District of Colorado under the AEA.
The court held that petitioners were likely to succeed on the merits because the proclamation exceeded the scope of the Alien Enemies Act.

Specifically, the court found that 'invasion' and 'predatory incursion' as used in the AEA require military action by a foreign nation or government, not criminal activity by a gang, and that TdA does not qualify as a 'foreign nation or government' under the statute.

The government appealed the TRO on April 23, 2025, but the Tenth Circuit denied its emergency motion for a stay on April 29, 2025, finding the government had not shown irreparable harm since all class members remained in federal custody.
The government voluntarily dismissed this appeal on May 12, 2025.
A second appeal of the preliminary injunction and class certification orders was filed on July 7, 2025, which remains pending as case number 25-1265.

The preliminary injunction prohibits the government from using the Alien Enemies Act to detain, transfer, or remove Venezuelan nationals from the District of Colorado based on alleged TdA membership, effectively blocking implementation of the presidential proclamation within the district.

The injunction remains in effect pending appeal, with the court determining that the government retains authority to prosecute crimes and remove individuals through normal immigration procedures under Title 8.
The petitioners, proceeding under the pseudonyms D.B.U. and R.M.M., were represented by the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation and the Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network.
They brought claims under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 alleging violations of the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause and challenging the statutory basis for invoking the Alien Enemies Act.

evidence: On March 31, 2025, the National Treasury Employees Union (NTEU) filed suit challenging Executive Order 14,251, which President Trump had issued on March 27, 2025.

The union, represented by its own legal counsel, sued the President and the heads of multiple federal agencies where NTEU represents workers, including the Departments of Treasury, Energy, Justice, Health and Human Services, and Interior, as well as the Environmental Protection Agency and Federal Communications Commission.

The Executive Order invoked 5 U.S.C. § 7103(b)(1) of the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute to exclude over thirty federal agencies and subdivisions from the statute's collective bargaining requirements, claiming these entities have "as a primary function intelligence, counterintelligence, investigative, or national security work."

NTEU brought three causes of action: two ultra vires claims alleging the Executive Order exceeded the President's statutory authority under Section 7103(b)(1) and Chapter 71 of Title 5, and a First Amendment retaliation claim.
NTEU filed a motion for preliminary injunction on April 4, 2025.
Following briefing and oral argument on April 23, Judge Friedman granted the preliminary injunction on April 25, with a detailed opinion following on April 28 (2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 80268).

The court found that NTEU had rebutted the presumption of regularity with "clear evidence" that the President's use of the national security exemption was motivated by retaliation against unions that challenged his agenda and a desire to make federal employees easier to fire, rather than genuine national security considerations.
The government appealed to the D.C. Circuit on April 29 and moved for a stay pending appeal.

Judge Friedman denied the stay motion on May 1, but on May 16, a divided D.C. Circuit panel granted the stay, finding that NTEU had not established irreparable harm because agencies had been advised not to terminate collective bargaining agreements until litigation concluded, though the panel noted individual units could seek relief if agencies deviated from this guidance.

Following the appellate stay, NTEU presented evidence that agencies were already violating their collective bargaining agreements by refusing to bargain, stopping dues deductions, and beginning to implement reductions in force.
This sweeping order affected approximately two-thirds of the federal workforce and about 65.9% of NTEU-represented employees (roughly 104,278 workers).
No previous president had used this narrow national security exemption to exclude entire Cabinet-level agencies from the statute.

The OPM Guidance explained that excluded agencies would no longer be subject to collective bargaining requirements and directed them on facilitating "large-scale reductions in force" and removing "underperforming employees."

A White House Fact Sheet stated that "[c]ertain Federal unions have declared war on President Trump's agenda" and distinguished between unions that are "constructive partners" versus those engaging in "mass obstruction."
The government also filed a preemptive lawsuit against an NTEU chapter in the Eastern District of Kentucky seeking to terminate NTEU's largest collective bargaining agreement with the IRS.

The government defended the Executive Order as within the President's discretion under the statute and argued the district court lacked jurisdiction because claims should be channeled through the Federal Labor Relations Authority, though NTEU countered that the Executive Order itself eliminated access to those administrative channels.

evidence: On February 11, 2025, current and former federal employees and two unions representing federal workers filed suit in the Southern District of New York against the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and entities associated with the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), including Elon Musk in his capacity as director.
the plaintiffs alleged violations of the Privacy Act of 1974 and sought declaratory and injunctive relief under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The case arose from events immediately following President Trump's inauguration on January 20, 2025, when he signed Executive Order 14,158 establishing DOGE to modernize federal technology and improve government efficiency.

That same day, OPM granted at least six individuals associated with DOGE immediate administrative access to multiple OPM systems containing the personally identifiable information of tens of millions of current and former federal employees, contractors, and job applicants.
These systems contained social security numbers, health records, banking information, security clearance data, and family member information.
Over the following weeks, additional DOGE agents received similar access, ultimately totaling at least twenty individuals.

The plaintiffs alleged that OPM violated the Privacy Act by disclosing records to individuals who were either not OPM employees or who lacked a legitimate need for the information in performing their duties.

The complaint detailed how OPM bypassed its normal security protocols: the DOGE agents had not received proper vetting or security clearances, several had not completed mandatory cybersecurity training before gaining access, and at least one individual had been fired from a private cybersecurity firm for allegedly leaking proprietary information.

Internal emails showed that access was granted on an emergency "911-esque" basis, with one official acknowledging they had "no immediate plans to change anything" when requesting urgent access for additional personnel.
After negative press coverage on February 6, 2025, OPM began removing some access privileges.
The case was initially assigned to Judge Victor Marrero but was reassigned to Judge Denise L. Cote on February 13, 2025.
The plaintiffs filed an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order on February 14, which was later converted to a motion for preliminary injunction at the parties' joint request.

Meanwhile, similar litigation proceeded in other districts, with a Maryland court issuing a temporary restraining order against OPM on February 24, 2025, later converted to a preliminary injunction (though stayed pending appeal by the Fourth Circuit).
On March 14, 2025, the defendants moved to dismiss the complaint, arguing the plaintiffs lacked standing and failed to state valid claims.

Judge Cote largely denied this motion on April 3, 2025, finding the plaintiffs had adequately alleged standing based on an injury analogous to the common law tort of intrusion upon seclusion, and had plausibly stated violations of the Privacy Act.

The court dismissed the plaintiffs' direct Privacy Act claims for damages but allowed them to proceed as predicates for their APA claims, noting that while the Privacy Act provides monetary remedies, it does not provide the injunctive relief plaintiffs sought except in narrow circumstances not applicable here.
Following expedited discovery and briefing, the plaintiffs filed a motion for preliminary injunction on April 25, 2025.
A hearing was held on May 29, 2025, during which OPM's Chief Information Officer Gregory Hogan testified and was cross-examined.
The evidence showed that OPM had granted administrative access to its systems to seventeen DOGE agents plus three OPM leadership officials.

While the government argued few individuals had actually logged into the systems, the court found this distinction irrelevant as the Privacy Act prohibits unauthorized disclosure regardless of actual use.

On June 9, 2025, Judge Cote issued a detailed opinion granting the preliminary injunction, finding the plaintiffs had demonstrated likelihood of success on their claims that OPM violated the Privacy Act by disclosing records to individuals without proper authorization or need, and by failing to maintain appropriate safeguards.

The court found OPM's rushed onboarding process, failure to follow security protocols, and granting of sweeping administrative access without demonstrated need constituted arbitrary and capricious agency action reviewable under the APA.
The court emphasized that OPM's departure from basic cybersecurity practices was "reminiscent of the failures that contributed to the 2015 data breach" that had affected over 21 million people.

The preliminary injunction, formally issued on June 20, 2025, required OPM to file within two weeks a report describing processes and procedures implemented since March 6, 2025, to ensure Privacy Act compliance for any new grants of access to records containing personally identifiable information.
The injunction was administratively stayed for fourteen days and conditioned on the plaintiffs posting a $1,000 bond.
The case remains ongoing, with the government ordered to complete the administrative record by August 29, 2025.
